extracted.intended_audience: research integrity community, journal editors, publishers, authors, and readers following retractions and publication ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying, investigating, and responding to suspected paper-mill or fabricated submissions (including detection of false authorship, AI-generated text, plagiarism, and other indicators of misconduct) and deciding corrective actions like retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unable to verify identity, contribution, affiliations, or origins
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal wording: the journal was “unable to verify the identity, contribution, or affiliations of a number of the authors listed on this manuscript, nor could the origins of the study be confirmed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a publisher cannot verify who the authors are, their contributions, affiliations, or the provenance of the study, this is a major red flag (often associated with paper mills) and is appropriate grounds for retraction or formal investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors must be aware of and consent to submission/publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported that two listed authors “were not aware of this submission nor consented to its publication.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should require explicit confirmation of authorship and consent from all listed authors prior to publication (e.g., email confirmation, signed authorship forms) and treat claims of non-consent as serious authorship misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify ORCID and other author identifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: An author said she never verified her ORCID ID with the journal before publication and requested removal of her name, which the journal refused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require and validate persistent author identifiers (ORCID) and cross-check them against institutional affiliations; failing to verify identifiers is an avoidable procedural lapse that can enable false authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for 'tortured phrases' and other signs of AI/LLM manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic on PubPeer noted several “tortured phrases” in the introduction — substitutions like ‘sustainability’ → ‘long-term viability’ and ‘mechanistic insights’ → ‘visual percepts into processes [of a chemical reaction].’ Such tortured phrases often indicate the use of AI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screen manuscripts for unnatural phrase substitutions, awkward synonyms, and other linguistic artifacts typical of LLM paraphrasing; such patterns are indicators of machine-generated or heavily machine-mediated text and warrant further scrutiny of provenance and authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism detection
rubrics_metrics.description: An investigator reported finding three instances of potential plagiarism in the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use similarity-detection tools and manual checks to identify copied text or unattributed reuse; multiple instances of plagiarism support strong corrective actions (expressions of concern, correction, or retraction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Check figure integrity and obvious mistakes in figures
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic wrote the “numerous obvious mistakes” in the figures of the paper “likely represent the greatest novelty and originality to be found in the whole manuscript.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine figures for fabrication, manipulation, duplicated elements, or blatant errors; figure problems can indicate deeper data provenance issues and should be investigated thoroughly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify relevance and correctness of references
rubrics_metrics.description: A PubPeer comment pointed out irrelevant and incorrect references in the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm that citations are relevant and accurately represented; irrelevant/mis-cited references may indicate sloppy assembly of manuscripts or intentional padding/citation manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect nonsensical or incorrect statements that undermine validity/authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Publisher notices said they “discovered instances of nonsensical or incorrect statements, raising questions about both the authorship and validity of the content presented.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonsensical claims, internally inconsistent reasoning, or factually incorrect statements are red flags for authorship and validity problems and justify deeper investigation and possible retraction if pervasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to authorship policies and publication ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Frontiers retracted a paper for a “serious breach of our authorship policies and of publication ethics.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals must enforce clear authorship criteria (contribution, approval, accountability) and other publication-ethics standards; serious breaches should trigger corrective actions per COPE/publisher policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to external alerts and post-publication peer review (e.g., PubPeer)
rubrics_metrics.description: A researcher (Lukas Koch) alerted the journal via email and PubPeer posts called out problems; these external reports prompted journal scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers and editors should have processes to triage and investigate credible external reports (PubPeer, direct emails from researchers) and act promptly when concerns about authorship, data, or text are raised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify institutional affiliations and claimed organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: The author’s LinkedIn listed a company (GenLab Biosolutions Private Limited) in India; the company’s Facebook hadn’t posted since 2023 and the website domain was defunct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-check claimed affiliations and organizational websites/records; false or unverifiable institutional ties are suspicious and can indicate fabricated author identities or dubious provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require transparency about third-party contributions and data provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: The author told a critic some of the structures were “made by a third party, as my chemistry colleague dropped out,” and admitted not knowing how to use the software to make reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandate disclosure of any third-party services, contractors, or external contributors (e.g., editing services, figure/data generators) and verify their role; undisclosed third-party involvement can mask paper-mill activity or fabricated data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use retraction when investigation confirms unresolvable provenance/authorship issues
rubrics_metrics.description: An investigation panel requested the retraction of 10 papers; multiple journals issued retraction notices citing inability to verify authorship/origins or nonsensical content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When provenance, authorship, or validity cannot be resolved and the integrity of the record is compromised, retraction is an appropriate remedy; retraction notices should explain the reasons transparently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track and report post-publication impact (citations) of problematic papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Some retracted or questioned papers had been cited (example: a sole-author 2022 paper cited 165 times; another paper cited over 600 times).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor citations to problematic or retracted work to assess downstream impact and notify citing authors/journals where appropriate; high citation counts increase urgency for clear corrective notices.
